explanation: Any switching arc is an ignition source in a combustible atmosphere. Leave electrical states as they are, evacuate, shut off gas, ventilate.

questionText: Propane leaks differ from natural gas leaks because propane:

choices.text: Is heavier than air and pools at floor level

explanation: LP sinks and accumulates low — changing both the hazard and where you test for it.

questionText: Kitchen gas manifold pressure is measured with a:

choices.text: Manometer, in inches of water column, while firing

explanation: Inches w.c. is the unit (28 in. w.c. ≈ 1 psi); the manometer connects at the appliance pressure tap with burners on.

questionText: Running natural-gas orifices on propane causes:

choices.text: Severe over-firing with sooting and rollout risk

explanation: Propane packs ~2.5x the energy per cubic foot at higher pressure — NG orifices pass far too much fuel.

questionText: A thermocouple holding a pilot safety valve generates approximately:
explanation: The pilot-heated junction produces tens of millivolts, just enough to hold the magnetic safety valve open.

questionText: Flame rectification proves a flame exists by:

choices.text: A microamp DC current conducted through the ionized flame to ground

explanation: The flame conducts asymmetrically, rectifying the sensor's AC to a small DC current the control counts in microamps.

questionText: An appliance that lights, runs seconds, then drops out repeatedly most often needs:

choices.text: Its flame sensor rod cleaned and burner ground verified

explanation: Oxide/grime on the rod chokes the microamp signal; the current also needs a sound ground path through the burner.

questionText: The purpose of ignition lockout after failed trials is to:

choices.text: Prevent unburned gas accumulating in the appliance and flue

explanation: Each failed trial dumps gas. Lockout stops the accumulation that repeated blind resets would create.

questionText: A healthy gas burner flame appears:

choices.text: Blue and stable with defined inner cones
Nearly invisible and lifting off the burner

explanation: Blue and stable indicates complete combustion; yellow/sooty flames are CO factories; lifting flames have excess air/velocity.

questionText: Air-free CO in commercial appliance flue gas approaching 400 ppm requires:
explanation: Elevated CO is an active hazard: correct the combustion problem or shut the appliance down before leaving.

questionText: Before leaving any gas job you must:

choices.text: Leak-test every fitting you disturbed with approved solution or detector

explanation: Every touched joint gets tested, every time. Gas leak discipline is what keeps kitchens standing.

questionText: A range top burner burns unevenly with flame missing along one side after a heavy boil-over. The fix is:

choices.text: Clean the carbonized burner ports with brush and port tool
Drill the ports one size larger

explanation: Boil-overs carbonize in ports and block them. Clean to restore the pattern — drilling oversizes the ports and permanently over-fires the burner.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A millivolt gas fryer is completely dead: pilot lights and holds, but the main burner never fires. Your meter should trace:

choices.text: Thermopile millivolts through the high-limit and thermostat to the gas valve coil

explanation: Millivolt systems are powered entirely by the thermopile. Voltage-drop the mV circuit through each safety and the thermostat to find the open or weak link.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A boiler combi throws repeated fill faults although water supply pressure is good. The classic cause is:
explanation: Level probes sense water conductivity; scale coating insulates them so the control never "sees" the water it has. Descale and clean the probes.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A combi runs long cook times with visible steam around the door edge. Before generator diagnosis, check:

choices.text: The door gasket and hinge adjustment

explanation: Steam escaping the door is capacity walking away. Gasket/hinge inspection takes minutes and explains the symptom directly.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: The most important preparation for servicing an unfamiliar combi model is:

choices.text: The model-specific service manual and diagnostic access codes

explanation: Combi architectures vary sharply by manufacturer. The service manual's diagnostics, menus, and procedures are primary tools on these machines.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

subcategory: Steam-Jacketed Kettles, Tilt Skillets, and Pressure Equipment
questionText: A self-contained steam-jacketed kettle heats slowly and its jacket gauge shows no vacuum cold. The kettle most likely needs:

choices.text: Air purged / jacket vacuum re-established and water charge verified per the manual

explanation: Air in the jacket ruins condensing heat transfer. The cold-vacuum reading is the tell; purge and recharge per procedure.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

subcategory: Steam-Jacketed Kettles, Tilt Skillets, and Pressure Equipment
questionText: The door interlock on a pressure steamer exists to:

choices.text: Prevent the door opening while the cavity is pressurized — preventing a steam explosion at the operator

explanation: Opening a pressurized compartment releases explosive steam at face level. The interlock chain is life-safety equipment, tested and never defeated.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: Blocked range burner ports after boil-overs should be:

choices.text: Cleaned with a brush and port tool

explanation: Cleaning restores the designed flame pattern; drilling permanently over-fires the burner.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A millivolt fryer control system is powered by:
explanation: The thermopile (hundreds of mV) powers valve, thermostat, and safeties — no external power at all.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: Soot at a gas fryer's flue outlets indicates:

choices.text: Combustion problems producing CO — inspect burners, air, and venting now

explanation: Soot is incomplete combustion made visible; treat as a combustion/CO problem, not cosmetics.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: The universal gas appliance diagnostic order is:

choices.text: Fuel path → ignition → flame proving → control chain

explanation: Verify gas supply and pressure, then lighting, then proving, then the control logic — the frame fits every gas appliance.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: The most destructive recurring problem in boiler-type combi ovens is:
explanation: Scale blinds probes, buries elements, and jams drains — water treatment plus descaling discipline is the combi's lifeline.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: Scale-coated level probes in a combi boiler cause:

choices.text: False fill/water faults because the control cannot sense water conductivity

explanation: Conductivity probes insulated by scale read "no water" regardless of actual level.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: Visible steam escaping a combi door during cooking means:

choices.text: Check gasket and hinges before deeper steam-system diagnosis

explanation: Door leaks bleed steam capacity and mimic generator weakness — the two-minute door inspection comes first.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A jacket safety valve on a steam kettle may be:

choices.text: Tested per procedure only — never plugged or bypassed
Replaced with a pipe plug temporarily
Adjusted to a higher pressure for faster cooking

explanation: It is pressure-vessel relief. Defeating it turns a kettle into a bomb; a dripping valve gets replaced, not plugged.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A defeated door interlock on a pressure steamer risks:

choices.text: An operator-level steam explosion when the door opens under pressure

explanation: The interlock prevents opening under pressure. Its defeat is a direct, severe injury hazard.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: When a kettle repair crosses into certified pressure-vessel/boiler work, the professional response is:

choices.text: Refuse gracefully and refer to appropriately licensed service
Have the customer sign a waiver

explanation: Licensing boundaries on pressure vessels exist in most jurisdictions — referring correctly protects everyone, including you.
referenceBookSection: Module 19 — Ranges, Combi Ovens & Specialty Equipment

questionText: A kitchen suffers mysterious pilot outages, doors that whistle, and smoke rolling out of the hood edges. The unifying cause is:

choices.text: Failed make-up air leaving the kitchen strongly negative

explanation: Negative building pressure starves pilots, spills hood capture, and backdrafts flues. Restore make-up air before chasing individual symptoms.

questionText: Mesh-style filters found installed in a Type I grease hood should be:

choices.text: Replaced with proper baffle filters — mesh is not permitted over grease equipment
Left if the customer prefers them

explanation: NFPA 96 requires baffle-type grease filters in Type I hoods; mesh loads with grease and becomes fuel above the fire.

questionText: The entire gas cook line is dead, but breakers and gas supply check fine. The overlooked suspect is:

choices.text: A failed hood exhaust interlock / proving switch that must run for cooking equipment to operate
The fire department shut the street gas

explanation: NFPA 96 interlocks cooking equipment to exhaust operation. A dead fan or failed proving switch disables the line by design.

questionText: During an unrelated fryer repair you notice heavy grease stalactites inside the hood plenum. You should:

choices.text: Scrape it quickly and move on
Document it and report it to the operator in writing as a fire hazard needing certified cleaning
Schedule yourself to clean the ducts

explanation: Duct/plenum grease is building-fire fuel. Reporting in writing protects lives and liability; certified exhaust cleaners do the remediation.

questionText: After a suppression discharge, the gas cook line will not restore even with breakers reset. The likely reason is:

choices.text: The suppression-linked mechanical gas valve tripped and must be reset/re-armed as part of system restoration

explanation: Discharge automatically closes the gas valve serving hood equipment. Restoration follows the licensed contractor's re-arming of the system.

questionText: A customer asks you to swap the fryer and the griddle positions under the hood. Beyond the utilities, you must:

choices.text: Nothing else — equipment placement is the customer's choice
Flag that suppression nozzle aiming is appliance-specific and the fire protection contractor must review the change
Re-aim the nozzles yourself to match
Remove the nozzle caps for better coverage

explanation: Nozzle-to-appliance alignment is part of the listed system design. Moving appliances without suppression review leaves the new arrangement unprotected.

questionText: Missing chrome caps on suppression nozzles over the char-broiler should be:

choices.text: Reported: caps keep grease from plugging nozzles, and plugged nozzles fail to discharge
Removed from the other nozzles for symmetry

explanation: Blow-off caps protect nozzle orifices from grease loading. A grease-plugged nozzle may not discharge over a fire — report for fire-protection service.

questionText: Type I hoods differ from Type II because they:

choices.text: Handle grease-laden vapor and require grease-rated ducts, filters, and suppression per NFPA 96

explanation: Grease changes everything: welded liquid-tight duct, baffle filters, fire suppression, and cleaning schedules.

questionText: Grease baffle filters must be oriented:

choices.text: Baffles vertical so collected grease drains to the troughs

explanation: Vertical baffles let inertially collected grease run down to the collection trough instead of pooling in the airstream.

questionText: A strongly negative kitchen (failed make-up air) causes:

choices.text: Pilot outages, smoke spill at hood edges, and flue backdrafting

explanation: Exhaust without make-up starves the space: combustion air, hood containment, and flue draft all suffer at once.

questionText: Kitchen exhaust duct interiors are cleaned by:

choices.text: Certified exhaust cleaning companies on NFPA 96 schedules

explanation: System-wide grease removal is a certified specialty on code-mandated frequency; techs document and report what they see.

questionText: The purpose of exhaust fan hinge kits is:

choices.text: Tipping the fan up so the duct and fan can actually be cleaned

explanation: Without a hinge kit the duct behind the fan never gets cleaned — a standard write-up item.

questionText: Cooking appliances under a Type I hood are interlocked so they:

choices.text: Cannot operate unless the exhaust system runs

explanation: NFPA 96 requires exhaust operation for cooking — a failed proving switch mimics a dead cook line.

questionText: Wet-chemical agent extinguishes grease fires by:

choices.text: Saponification — converting the burning grease surface to a sealing soap foam

explanation: The potassium agent reacts with hot grease to form foam that cools and seals against reflash — the UL 300 principle.

questionText: Fusible links in a suppression system:

choices.text: Melt at rated temperature to trigger discharge

explanation: The links are the thermal detection: fire heat melts them, releasing the mechanism.

questionText: Recharging suppression tanks and replacing fusible links is work for:
explanation: Fire suppression maintenance is licensed, code-scheduled work — a bright-line boundary for equipment techs.

questionText: After a suppression discharge, equipment under the hood may return to service:

choices.text: As soon as it is wiped down
Only after the licensed contractor recharges and re-arms the system (and gas/power are properly restored)

explanation: The kitchen is unprotected until the system is recharged and re-armed; gas valves and shunt trips restore as part of that process.

questionText: The sanitizing proof for a high-temp machine is:

choices.text: A thermolabel or max-registering thermometer confirming 160°F at the dish surface

explanation: Gauges read water in the pipe; codes care about dish-surface temperature. The thermolabel through a cycle is the accepted proof.

questionText: A low-temp machine washing well but failing sanitizer test strips most likely has:

choices.text: An empty sanitizer container or failed/airlocked dosing pump

explanation: Low-temp sanitizing is pure chemistry: no chlorine reaching the rinse means no sanitizing, and the dosing system is the suspect chain.

subcategory: Heat: Tanks, Boosters, and Temperature Complaints
questionText: A high-temp machine rinses at 145°F. Incoming water to the booster measures 105°F. The correct conclusion is:

choices.text: The building water heater is delivering low water — a healthy booster can only add ~40°F
The machine needs a bigger booster

explanation: Boosters are sized for roughly a 40°F rise. 105 + 40 = 145: the booster is doing its job on starved input. Fix the building hot water first.

subcategory: Heat: Tanks, Boosters, and Temperature Complaints
questionText: A booster's rinse temperature has drifted down over two months and one element has failed. The underlying condition to fix is:

choices.text: Scale accumulation on elements and tank — delime and address water treatment

explanation: Scale insulates elements (falling performance) and overheats them (rotating failures). New elements without deliming repeat the cycle.

questionText: Ware exits with a white film. Vinegar on a test plate dissolves it instantly. The film is:

choices.text: Mineral scale/hard-water film — water treatment and rinse-aid are the fix path

explanation: Acid-soluble white film is mineral. Check softener/treatment status and rinse-aid delivery; detergent residue would ignore the vinegar.

questionText: A conveyor machine washes poorly though pumps and temps check out. Several zone curtains are missing. The curtains matter because:

choices.text: They are cosmetic splash guards only
They separate zones — without them wash and rinse water cross-contaminate and spray patterns collapse
They hold heat in the vent hood

explanation: Curtains are functional zone barriers. Missing curtains let detergent wash into the rinse and sprays short-circuit — poor results with healthy machinery.

questionText: A dish machine "will not start" with power confirmed. The first component to check is:
explanation: The door interlock is the gate for everything and takes the most physical abuse. It is the #1 no-start cause on dish machines.

questionText: High-temp machines sanitize with:

choices.text: A 180°F final rinse achieving 160°F at the dish surface

explanation: Heat sanitizing: 180°F rinse design, proven by 160°F at the ware surface.

questionText: Low-temp machines sanitize with:

choices.text: Chlorine sanitizer dosed at ~50-100 ppm in the final rinse

explanation: Chemical sanitizing replaces heat: chlorine concentration verified by test strips.

questionText: The booster heater's job is to:

choices.text: Raise final-rinse water roughly 40°F to sanitizing temperature

explanation: The booster lifts building hot water (~140°F) to the 180°F rinse — and can only add about 40°F.

questionText: Rinse temperature 40°F low with a healthy booster usually traces to:

choices.text: Low incoming water temperature from the building heater

explanation: Boosters amplify what they receive. Starved incoming water is the first check on low-rinse-temp calls.

questionText: The heaviest scale burden in the kitchen is found in:

choices.text: Booster heaters and dish machine tanks

explanation: Hottest water + constant throughput = fastest scaling. Deliming belongs in every dish machine PM.

questionText: A detergent conductivity probe coated in grease causes:

choices.text: No detergent dosing — the probe forever reads "enough"

explanation: The coated probe reports adequate conductivity regardless of actual detergent, so the pump never doses.

questionText: Greasy redeposit on washed ware points to:

choices.text: Exhausted wash-tank water or under-dosed detergent

explanation: Saturated tank water re-paints soil onto ware — tank change discipline and dosing verification are the fixes.

questionText: The most common cause of a no-start dish machine is:

choices.text: The door switch or latch not engaging

explanation: The abused door interlock gates the entire cycle — always the first check.

questionText: A machine that fills, then immediately loses its water usually has:

choices.text: A drain valve/flapper failing to seal

explanation: Water in, water straight out: the drain seal is the leak path to check first.

questionText: A conveyor machine "stuck" mid-cycle that resumes after several minutes may be:

choices.text: Waiting on rinse temperature from a starved or scaled booster

explanation: Temperature-hold logic pauses cycles until sanitizing temp is available — a heat problem wearing a control-problem costume.

questionText: A brewer produces weak coffee; the spray head shows heavy scale with only the center holes open. The mechanism of the weak brew is:

choices.text: Channeling — water pours down the center of the grounds bed instead of showering evenly

explanation: A scaled spray head concentrates flow through the middle, under-extracting the outer bed. Descale/replace the spray head and audit water treatment.

questionText: An espresso machine's pump gauge reads 6 bar at the group instead of 9. Before replacing the pump you should:

choices.text: Check for scale restriction in the flow path and verify against a blind-filter pressure test
Change the water filter housing O-ring

explanation: Scale restrictions mimic pump wear. A blind-filter (backflush) test isolates true pump output from flow-path losses.

questionText: A soft-serve machine leaks product into the drip tray after last night's cleaning. The most likely cause is:

choices.text: A missing or mis-seated shaft/door O-ring from reassembly

explanation: Post-cleaning leaks are assembly casualties: verify every seal and O-ring seat before deeper diagnosis. It is the #1 soft-serve service pattern.

questionText: A granita machine serves watery product; its condenser coil is packed with dust. The chain of cause is:

choices.text: Blocked condenser → poor refrigeration → cylinder cannot freeze product to consistency

explanation: Module 13's first law returns: a suffocated condenser cannot reject heat, so the cylinder never reaches consistency. Clean the coil, then re-evaluate.

questionText: Every flavor on a soda tower pours flat, and drinks feel barely cool. The unified diagnosis is:

choices.text: All syrup pumps failed at once
The chiller/cold plate has failed — warm water cannot hold carbonation

explanation: One failure explaining all flavors: carbonation collapses in warm water. Fix the chilling, and the "flat" complaint resolves.

questionText: Before working in a back room housing a bulk CO2 tank, the professional precaution is:

choices.text: Heed the CO2 monitor / ventilate — CO2 displaces air silently and asphyxiates

explanation: CO2 is heavier than air, invisible, and silent. Monitors exist because techs and staff have died in syrup rooms — alarm or breathlessness means leave and ventilate.

questionText: Weak coffee from a brewer with a heavily scaled spray head is caused by:

choices.text: Channeled water flow under-extracting the grounds bed

explanation: Scale closes outer spray holes; water pours down the bed's center and under-extracts the rest.

questionText: Espresso machine boiler elements are interlocked to water level because:

choices.text: Dry-firing destroys the element and boiler

explanation: An element exposed by low water overheats instantly — the interlock is boiler protection.

questionText: An espresso pump reading low pressure should first be checked against:

choices.text: Scale restriction via a blind-filter test isolating pump output from flow-path losses

explanation: Scale mimics pump wear; the blind-filter test separates the two before parts are ordered.

questionText: Straight RO water is often wrong for coffee because:

choices.text: Some mineral content is needed for proper extraction and flavor

explanation: Beverage treatment aims for controlled minerality, not zero — brew chemistry needs some hardness.

questionText: Soft-serve machines that "fail" the morning after cleaning most often have:

choices.text: Reassembly errors: mis-seated beaters, missing O-rings, misassembled valves

explanation: Daily teardown means daily reassembly risk — verify assembly before condemning components.

questionText: Icy, coarse texture from a frozen beverage machine suggests:

choices.text: Worn beater/scraper blades or consistency set too hard / low mix

explanation: Scraping and consistency control make smooth product; worn blades and over-hard settings make ice.

questionText: Soft-serve product too soft with a grease-blanketed condenser is explained by:

choices.text: The refrigeration side failing to freeze — clean the condenser first

explanation: The kitchen's first law again: suffocated condensers cannot freeze product to spec.

questionText: Soda pouring as all syrup with no fizz from every valve indicates:

choices.text: Carbonated water side down: CO2, carbonator pump/probe, or water supply

explanation: The common element across all valves is the soda-water supply — the carbonation chain is the suspect.

questionText: Drink ratio (water:syrup) is verified with:

choices.text: A brix cup or ratio device measuring both streams at the valve

explanation: The ratio cup catches both streams; valve flow controls adjust to the spec (commonly ~5:1).

questionText: The CO2 hazard in beverage back rooms is:
explanation: CO2 quietly fills enclosed spaces from the floor up. Monitors, ventilation, and leaving when alarmed are the discipline.

subcategory: Inputs, Outputs, and the Control Board
questionText: An oven overshoots wildly. Its NTC thermistor probe measures 40kΩ at room temperature; the chart says it should read 10kΩ. The correct action is:

choices.text: Replace the probe (and inspect its connector) — the board is acting correctly on false data
Adjust the offset until it cooks right

explanation: A probe reading far off-chart feeds the board fiction. The board responds correctly to wrong data — fix the data source.

subcategory: Inputs, Outputs, and the Control Board
questionText: A board shows the heat cycle active but its heat output terminal measures 0V with all safeties closed. Before condemning the board:

choices.text: Verify every interlock condition in the manual's output logic — many "dead outputs" are the logic honoring an unsatisfied condition
Jumper the output to test the contactor

explanation: Boards withhold outputs when any required condition (door, fan proving, temperature window, time delay) is unmet. Read the ladder before replacing the computer.

subcategory: Inputs, Outputs, and the Control Board
questionText: The most common reason a replacement control board fails within weeks is:

choices.text: The root cause that killed the first board (water ingress, shorted load, overvoltage) was never found

explanation: Boards are usually victims, not causes. Diagnose the murder weapon or the replacement inherits it.

subcategory: Error Codes, Diagnostics, and Service Modes
questionText: A fryer intermittently resets mid-shift; error history shows resets cluster at 11:45am daily. Supply voltage at the fryer measures 189V during the lunch rush (rated 208V). The diagnosis is:

choices.text: Building voltage sag under rush load — an electrical supply problem, not an appliance fault

explanation: Brownouts reset control electronics on schedule with kitchen load. The error history found the pattern; the meter found the cause.

subcategory: Error Codes, Diagnostics, and Service Modes
questionText: The fastest way to test whether a combi's drain pump itself works is:

choices.text: Actuate the pump directly from the service menu's output test

explanation: Manual output actuation runs the component on command — isolating it from cycle logic and interlocks in seconds.

questionText: A chain's connected fryer stopped reporting to its dashboard the week the store replaced its router. The first check is:

choices.text: The appliance's network status screen and re-joining it to the new network
The cloud service status page only

explanation: The timeline names the suspect: new router, new credentials. Network-side causes dominate connectivity failures.

questionText: Remote telemetry shows a walk-in climbing from 36°F to 50°F between 2-6am with the compressor running continuously. Before arrival, the strongest hypothesis is:

choices.text: Staff left the door open all night
A capacity-side fault (dirty condenser, low charge, iced evaporator) — running-but-losing points at capacity, not control

explanation: Continuous running with rising temperature is a machine trying and failing — capacity-side faults. A door event would show recovery after closing; control faults show not-running.

questionText: The diagnostic order for control-system faults is:

choices.text: Inputs (sensors/switches), outputs, then the board itself

explanation: Inputs fail most and make healthy boards act insane; outputs next; the board itself is the last suspect.

questionText: An NTC thermistor's resistance:
explanation: Negative Temperature Coefficient: verify against the chart with an ohmmeter.

questionText: Board output terminal shows proper voltage but the motor does not run. The fault is:

choices.text: External: wiring, contactor, or the motor itself

explanation: Voltage delivered = board did its job. The Module 11 load chain takes over from there.

questionText: Before unplugging connectors on a control board you should:

choices.text: Kill power and photograph the connector layout

explanation: Live disconnection kills boards; photos prevent reassembly errors that create second faults.

questionText: An error code tells you:

choices.text: The condition the board detected — cause still requires verification

explanation: Codes are testimony, not verdicts: verify the sensed condition with instruments, then trace cause.

questionText: Service-mode error history is most valuable for:

choices.text: Converting intermittent complaints into time-stamped patterns

explanation: Timestamps and counts turn "it sometimes dies" into "it dies at every lunch rush" — a diagnosable pattern.

questionText: A unit "broken since install" that behaves as if built for different conditions likely has:

choices.text: Wrong configuration (voltage/gas/altitude/units) — verify config against the data plate

explanation: Configuration sets the appliance's personality; mis-set menus mimic hardware defects from day one.

questionText: Ghost resets and scrambled displays across an appliance's controls suggest checking first:

choices.text: Supply voltage under load, grounding, moisture, and compartment heat

explanation: Environment kills kitchen electronics: brownouts, bad grounds, pressure-washer water, and grease-blocked cooling.

questionText: A connected appliance that stopped reporting after site IT changes should first be checked at:

choices.text: Its own network status screen / rejoining the network

explanation: Network-side causes dominate: credentials and routers change; radios rarely die on schedule with IT work.

questionText: Telemetry showing continuous compressor run with climbing box temperature indicates:

choices.text: A capacity-side fault: condenser, charge, or airflow

explanation: Trying-but-losing is capacity; not-trying is control. Remote data sorts the call before the truck rolls.

subcategory: Why PM Sells and What It Contains
questionText: The strongest honest argument for a kitchen PM contract is:

choices.text: Most catastrophic kitchen failures are slow, visible accumulations that scheduled visits catch cheaply

explanation: Dirty condensers, scale, worn gaskets, greasy bearings: the killers accumulate visibly. PM interrupts them at a fraction of downtime cost.

subcategory: Why PM Sells and What It Contains
questionText: PM frequency should be set by:

choices.text: Each site's duty and conditions — grease load, water quality, hours, and equipment mix

explanation: Quarterly is the workhorse baseline, but the yeast-heavy bakery's ice machine and the grease-heavy grill's condensers earn monthly attention.

questionText: Three months after your PM report noted "compressor start components weakening, replacement recommended — declined by manager," the walk-in fails overnight. Your documentation:

choices.text: Protects your company and frames the failure as a declined recommendation, not negligence
Should be revised after the fact

explanation: Dated findings with declined recommendations are exactly why PM documentation exists — for the customer's planning and everyone's protection.

questionText: A customer insists a failed 3-year-old fryer element "must be warranty." The professional response is:

choices.text: Verify model/serial, install date, and warranty terms before making any commitment
Split the difference on the bill

explanation: Warranty is a verifiable fact, not a negotiation. Unverified promises become someone's unplanned expense — usually yours.

questionText: The economic case for PM rests on:

choices.text: Scheduled visits costing far less than emergency failures plus downtime and product loss

explanation: One prevented walk-in failure or line-down event pays for a year of visits.

questionText: The single most failure-preventing PM task in kitchens is:

choices.text: Cleaning condenser coils (and the airflow they need)

explanation: The grease-dusted condenser is the #1 root cause in kitchen refrigeration — PM interrupts it on schedule.

questionText: High-temp dish machine PM must document:

choices.text: Final-rinse sanitizing proof (temperature at the ware)

explanation: Sanitizing proof is the health-code heart of the machine — measured and written every visit.

questionText: Water treatment cartridges on PM programs are:

choices.text: Dated, changed on schedule, and documented — they protect everything downstream

explanation: Exhausted treatment quietly executes steamers, boosters, combis, and ice machines. The cartridge date is cheap insurance.

questionText: A noted-but-declined PM recommendation should be:

choices.text: Documented with date and the decline — it protects both parties later

explanation: The dated, declined recommendation is the professional record when the predicted failure arrives.

questionText: Service agreement "edges" a tech must know are:

choices.text: What is covered vs billable vs quote-first for the equipment in front of them

explanation: Whether this repair is covered work changes what you do next — knowing is part of the job.

questionText: Before telling a customer a repair is under warranty you must:

choices.text: Verify model/serial, install date, and terms

explanation: Warranty is verifiable fact; premature promises become unfunded costs.

questionText: On warranty repairs, root-cause diagnosis is:

choices.text: Still mandatory, or the replacement fails and the claim repeats

explanation: Warranty replaces victims; your diagnosis still has to catch the killer (scale, voltage, water, airflow).

questionText: Photos on PM and repair tickets are:

choices.text: Cheap, decisive documentation of conditions found and work done

explanation: A photo of the grease-blanketed coil or the scale-buried element settles every later question.

questionText: The commercial loop PM documentation feeds is:

choices.text: Condition reports → approved repairs → trust → renewed agreements

explanation: Honest, documented findings are how PM programs grow — the paperwork is the product.

questionText: A 12-component control chain shows an open somewhere. Split-half search finds it in at most:
explanation: 12 → 6 → 3 → 1-2: binary search collapses chains logarithmically. Test the middle, not the ends.

questionText: You replace three parts at once and the fryer works. The problem with this "win" is:

choices.text: You learned nothing, billed for two innocent parts, and cannot answer which fix holds when it recurs

explanation: Shotgun repairs destroy the information the fault contained. One variable at a time is slower per step and faster per truth.

questionText: The step that keeps a correct repair from failing again in eight weeks is:

choices.text: Root-cause analysis — identifying what killed the failed component

explanation: Elements die of scale, boards die of water, compressors die of condensers. Replace the victim AND arrest the killer.

questionText: Since Tuesday: the walk-in runs warm, the prep table struggles, and the ice machine's production halved. The diagnostic question to ask FIRST is:

choices.text: What do all three share, and what changed Tuesday (ambient heat, condenser airflow, power)?

explanation: Three refrigeration victims with one onset date share an environmental cause — find Tuesday's change before opening three sealed systems.

questionText: A 9-year-old reach-in (typical life ~10-12 years) needs a $900 compressor; replacement is $2,400. The professional move is:

choices.text: Just do the repair — it is authorized work
Present both numbers with age and history honestly and let the customer decide
Recommend replacement to raise the ticket

explanation: Repair-vs-replace is the customer's economic decision, made well only when the tech frames the numbers honestly.

questionText: The correct first step on any service call is:

choices.text: Define and verify the complaint precisely — reproduce and measure it

explanation: You cannot fix what you have not observed; precise definition halves the diagnosis.

questionText: Every kitchen appliance localizes into the subsystems:
explanation: Power/fuel in, conversion to heat/cold/motion, distribution by air/water/refrigerant, governed by controls — the universal decomposition.

questionText: Split-half diagnosis means:

choices.text: Testing the middle of a chain so each measurement halves the search space
Checking half the appliance per visit

explanation: Binary search on any chain: logarithmic instead of linear hunting.

questionText: A swap-test is valid when:

choices.text: Identical adjacent equipment lets a suspect part move and the fault follow (or not)

explanation: Twin fryer banks and matched valves let the fault vote: it follows the guilty part.

questionText: Changing several parts at once is poor practice because:

choices.text: It destroys causal information, bills innocents, and leaves recurrence unexplainable

explanation: One variable at a time preserves the information the fault contains.

questionText: A correct repair without root-cause analysis:

choices.text: Leaves the killer in place — the replacement dies on the same schedule

explanation: Scale, water, airflow, and voltage kill again unless arrested.

questionText: Multi-symptom calls across several machines are best opened by asking:

choices.text: What do the victims share, and what changed at symptom onset?

explanation: Shared-cause reasoning: environment, water, power, and airflow serve many machines at once.

questionText: A whole cook line dead with good breakers should immediately suggest:

choices.text: A shared upstream cause — like the hood exhaust interlock/proving switch

explanation: NFPA 96 interlocks kill the line by design when exhaust proving fails — the classic shared-cause trap.

questionText: Repair-vs-replace framing belongs to:

choices.text: Honest numbers — repair cost, unit age/life, failure history, refrigerant status, downtime — with the customer deciding

explanation: The tech frames facts; the customer owns the economic decision.

questionText: The habit that builds diagnostic mastery over years is:

choices.text: Reviewing each interesting call: what was the earliest evidence and the faster path?

explanation: The post-call review grows the pattern library that lets veterans smell the fault from the doorway.

questionText: A new fryer's data plate says 240V/3Ø; the receptacle measures 208V/3Ø. The commissioning action is:

choices.text: Start it anyway — it will just run a little slow
Stop and resolve the supply mismatch now — element output and warranty both depend on it
Swap elements for 208V versions yourself and continue

explanation: Commissioning exists to catch exactly this. Starting up a mismatched unit certifies chronic complaints and a warranty argument.

questionText: Recording baseline readings (temps, pressures, amps) at startup matters because:

choices.text: It documents what THIS healthy unit reads — the reference every future diagnosis will wish it had

explanation: A documented healthy baseline turns future "is this reading normal?" questions into lookups instead of guesses.

questionText: The highest-leverage ten minutes at a new equipment handoff is spent on:

choices.text: Training the actual daily operators on operation, cleaning boundaries, and call-service triggers

explanation: Operator behavior drives year-one service history. The NEVER list and the quick-card prevent the most common, least profitable calls.

questionText: During commissioning you find the site electrician landed the new combi on an undersized breaker. You should:

choices.text: Fix the breaker yourself to finish the job
Document the deficiency, assign it to the electrical scope in writing, and state what is limited until corrected
Start the unit and let the breaker prove itself

explanation: Deficiency handling: found, documented, routed to the owning trade, with interim limits stated. Professional, in writing, no drama.

questionText: Commissioning begins with:

choices.text: Verifying the installation (utilities, placement, code items) against the data plate before power-on

explanation: Startup on a bad install certifies future failures — verification comes first.

questionText: The voltage check at commissioning catches:

choices.text: The 208/240 mismatch that otherwise becomes years of "slow equipment" complaints

explanation: Supply-vs-data-plate mismatch is born at installation and cheapest to fix on day one.

questionText: Food equipment drains require:

choices.text: An air gap to prevent backflow contamination

explanation: The air gap is a code-required backflow barrier between food equipment and drainage.

questionText: Relocating cooking appliances under a hood requires suppression review because:

choices.text: The hood may be too small
Nozzle aiming is appliance-specific in the listed design
The gas flex may be short

explanation: Module 20's rule surfaces at commissioning: nozzle-to-appliance alignment is part of the fire system design.

questionText: Startup baseline documentation should include:

choices.text: Operating temps, pressures, amp draws, and combustion values while the unit is new and right

explanation: The healthy baseline is the reference every future diagnosis will lean on.

questionText: Commissioning is complete when:

choices.text: The machine has performed its real job once, measured (full cycle, sanitizing/temperature proof as applicable)

explanation: Real work, measured, in front of you — not just lights and fans.

questionText: Handoff training should be delivered to:

choices.text: The people who actually operate and clean the machine daily

explanation: The opening cook and closing dishwasher determine the machine's service history.

questionText: The explicit NEVER list for operators includes:

choices.text: Never pressure-wash controls or hose electrical compartments

explanation: Water intrusion from aggressive cleaning is a leading killer of kitchen control electronics.

questionText: An installation deficiency found at commissioning is handled by:

choices.text: Documenting it, assigning it to the owning scope in writing, and stating interim limits
Ignoring it if the unit runs

explanation: Route it to the right trade, on paper, with consequences stated — professionalism without drama.

questionText: The signed commissioning report functions as:

choices.text: The machine's service-life birth certificate: verification, baseline, proof, and training record

explanation: It anchors warranty, future diagnosis, and the service relationship in one signed document.
